a staff session row lasting beyond 12 hours, or pairing an account with another account's key, is refused by the database); sign-in (a live staff key only, a response without a user handle or with another account's refused, user verification required, an assertion without UV or with BE or BS refused after the signature, a revoked key, a demoted account, a deleted account, ten unsigned responses naming a key's credential id leaving its owner able to sign in); the counter rule (a regression at sign-in and at step-up revokes the key and every staff session it opened, the current one included, and writes `staff_key_counter_regression`, its audit row and the `staff_key_suspect` mail); relying parties (a staff-key assertion made for the app's relying party and a personal-passkey assertion made for the console's are both refused on the relying-party check; one test runs with both relying party IDs `localhost`, the development configuration, and shows that the tables alone refuse a personal passkey at the console and a staff key at the app, and that each kind's registration options then exclude the account's credentials of the other kind); sessions (idle and absolute limits with the clock; an unmarked request that neither slides the idle expiry nor moves `last_used_at`, so a session read only by unmarked requests ends 15 minutes after the last marked one; a marked request that slides it, never past the absolute expiry; a revocation, a suspect key, a demotion and a take-down each refused at the session's next request; the stored browser label; the cookies' flags and their 12-hour Max-Age; both cookies cleared on `staff_session_required`; the host and origin checks; CSRF); lifecycle (grant-role to `user` revokes every staff key and staff session and deletes unused enrolments, and a later grant back to staff revives no key; a change between `moderator` and `admin` revokes staff sessions and enrolments and keeps keys; `revoke ... all` deletes unused enrolments and writes `staff_enrollments_cancelled`; an enrolment verified after `revoke ... all`, a demotion or a deletion enrols nothing; the take-down revokes the account's staff keys and staff sessions, deletes its enrolments, blanks its keys' names, AAGUIDs and transports, and writes its audit rows after `account_deleted`, in `takeDown` and in `finishTakeDown`; the janitor deletes staff sessions 30 days after they end and enrolments a day after use or expiry, and never a live one); mails (each of the four staff mails sent where section 7 says and nowhere else; `revoke ... all` on an account with only an unused enrolment writes `staff_enrollments_cancelled` and mails nothing; a counter regression appends `staff_key_counter_regression` and mails `staff_key_suspect`, never `passkey_suspect`; the templates pinned in `apps/api/test/mail/templates.test.ts`, none containing a URL); step-up (bound to action and target, single use, expiry, the wrong key, the counter rule; the params binding is a unit test in 3a, above).
- **Integration (audit)**: every staff action writes one row with the chain. Parity: rows with the test vectors' contents, written through the trigger from a session with a non-UTC `TimeZone` and `DateStyle` 'SQL, DMY', recompute in `chain.ts` to the stored hashes. Concurrency: several sessions insert at once, some inside transactions, and `audit-verify`, run while they insert and again after, passes walking `chain_seq`. An insert naming an existing id with `ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING` is written under a new id and chained; supplied `id`, `created_at`, `chain_version`, `chain_seq`, `prev_hash` and `hash` are overwritten; a temporary `audit_head` that `korbat_api` creates changes nothing. `korbat_api` cannot UPDATE, DELETE or TRUNCATE `audit_log`, nor write or lock `audit_head`, set `session_replication_role` or disable the trigger. With the head row missing, an insert fails with `the audit head is missing`. As the owner `korbat_migrate` (the test environment has no superuser URL): a row changed alone fails a plain `audit-verify`; a row changed with every later hash and the head recomputed passes a plain one and fails against a pair kept before the change. Every audit test that writes a row `audit-verify` must refuse runs inside one transaction that ends in a rollback and hands that transaction to the verifier's check, so no later file sees a broken chain: the parity rows (their step-up is signed by no stored key), the rows changed as the owner, a step-up action's row without an assertion, a key without its `staff_key_added` row and the missing head. Fixtures create staff keys only through the enrolment flow and `auth.add_staff_key`, and step-up rows only through the step-up flow. `global-setup.ts` inserts the head row `(1, 0, 64 zeros)` as `korbat_migrate` right after its truncate. Each auth-side fact's audit row commits and rolls back with its change (an error thrown after `auth.append_audit` leaves neither); `auth.append_audit` refuses an action outside its list; `audit-verify` passes a genuine step-up, with `CONSOLE_ORIGIN` unset too, and fails, naming the step-up check, when the row's params, target or session are changed as the owner or the assertion is moved to another row, each with every later hash and the head recomputed as in the rewrite test, when a row of a step-up action carries no assertion (under a staff, a demoted or the system actor), and when the assertion's key belongs to another account; it fails when a key has no `staff_key_added` row; grant-role's change and row are one transaction. The back-fill of 0012 is checked by the dry run, since the integration database holds no row older than 0012 (`scripts/test-db.mjs` migrates it and `global-setup.ts` then truncates every table): the dry run migrates the scratch database, which holds grant-role rows written before 0012, and runs `staff.js audit-verify` on it, which must pass.
- **HTTP**: the staff routes through the app with both origins configured: 404 with the console off; the app's session cookie and a bearer token refused on staff routes; a staff cookie refused on the app's routes; the no-store header; a console POST (the console's Host and Origin, the staff CSRF header) sent with the app's session and CSRF cookies present reaches the staff route and is not answered `csrf_failed`; no answer under `/api/staff/` carries an `Access-Control-*` header, even to an Origin listed in `TRUSTED_ORIGINS`; a GET with `Sec-Fetch-Site: same-site` or `cross-site`, or with an Origin other than `CONSOLE_ORIGIN`, is refused and leaves the session's idle expiry unchanged; a request with another Host answers 404; the route table holds no route of another module under `/api/staff`; at enrolment, sign-in and step-up, a spent challenge, a challenge of another purpose, one with another binding and a response with a bad signature each answer a staff code, never a `passkey_*` one, and at sign-in a bad signature on a live key and an unknown key get the same answer; `GET /api/staff/audit?at=` answers the page whose newest row is at that place. The integration client's `Browser` (`apps/api/test/integration/http-client.ts`, which today always echoes into `x-csrf-token`, `:40-41`) takes, besides its origin, a base URL and the names of the CSRF cookie it echoes and of the header it echoes it in. It requests `base + path` and sends the base's host as `Host`, since behind Caddy `@hono/node-server` builds the request's URL from the Host header. A console client therefore carries the console's host and origin and echoes `__Host-korbat_staff_csrf` in `x-staff-csrf`; the existing clients keep `http://localhost` and echo `__Host-korbat_csrf` in `x-csrf-token`.
- **Console**: server-rendered checks of each screen and source scans, as the app's tests do; the idle timer with a fake clock (restart on a marked success, the read at 13 minutes, another tab's activity moving the end, the warning and "Stay signed in", the timer set to the absolute end when that is nearer and its warning without the button, sign-in in place on 401 returning to the path); the fetch wrapper sends the activity mark only when a caller asks for it; the check of step-up options (a challenge of another length or purpose, a binding for another action, target, params or session handle, and an allow list of more than one key, each refused before `navigator.credentials.get`); the home screen reading sign-ins back to 7 days; "Go to place"; the Signal API call made only when `rpShared` is false. A browser check is committed with the console (`apps/admin/test/browser/`, run by `pnpm --filter @korbat/admin test:browser`). It builds the console. A small Node server then serves `dist` with the headers of Caddy's console site, the CSP read from `infra/caddy/Caddyfile` so the two cannot drift. The same server answers `/api/staff/*` from fixtures whose user-written strings are hostile: markup, `javascript:` URLs, bidirectional overrides and the longest names allowed. The check drives Chromium through playwright-core with a CDP virtual authenticator (device-bound and user-verifying) over every screen: enrolment, sign-in, home, a session revoked with the key, a step-up whose options bind another action refused before the key is asked, the audit log and the ended session. It fails on any `securitypolicyviolation` event, any CSP or Trusted Types console message, any DevTools CSP issue, any page error and any dialog (the channels of `console-lab.md` section 2). It needs no database and writes nothing, so CI runs it with the runner's own Chrome and the dry run runs it on each build. 3c adds its screens and payloads to it. The dry run also walks the console against the scratch stack: an enrolment with the virtual authenticator set to backup-eligible, refused and explained, after which the same link from the command line enrols a device-bound key; sign-in; sessions listed; one revoked with the key; and the audit log read. That walk-through stays in the scratch tooling, since it writes to the database it runs against.
- **Smoke**: the smoke test takes `--console <url>`, required like `--base`. The console's page answers with the exact CSP and `Cache-Control: no-store, no-transform`, and `/api/staff/me` answers 404 on the app's host and 401 `staff_session_required` on the console's.

## 14. Success criteria

1. Nothing gives staff powers but a staff session on the console's origin from a staff key whose authenticator reported UV and no BE, and every test in section 11's list passes.
2. Staff keys exist only through enrolments the command line issued, which the database enforces; keys are revoked from the command line (`staff.js revoke` or a demotion by grant-role), by an account's take-down, or by a counter regression, which also marks them suspect; and every enrolment issued or cancelled, key, sign-in, sign-out, revocation and role change is in the audit log, written in the same transaction as its change.
3. The audit log is a hash chain the API role can only extend, in an order and at times the database alone sets; `audit-verify` recomputes it in its own code, and a change made by any role, the owner and the superuser included, to a row at or before a kept head is detected when `audit-verify` runs with that head; and every row of a step-up action in it carries an assertion that `audit-verify` checks against the public key of a key its actor holds.
4. The console runs under the strict policy of section 3 with no violation in the committed browser check of section 12, over every screen with hostile fixtures, and renders every user string as text.
5. The app is unchanged for everyone but staff, whose staff powers are gone from it.

## 15. Amendments from the dry run (2026-10-01)

Found while the tasks were dry-run in the scratch clone, by the conformance review of each task, by the adversarial review of the range and by a walk-through in a real browser; each is applied in the prompts. Where an amendment and a section above differ, the amendment is current.

- **"Has a handle" is the auth side's record (section 6, `auth.add_staff_key`).** The function checks `auth.users.onboarded_at is not null`, which onboarding sets right after the profile and its handle exist; it never reads `public.profiles`.
- **One policy per staff table (section 6).** Each auth staff table has one `FOR ALL` policy for `korbat_auth`; a single narrower policy cannot serve the reads, updates and deletes the role needs, and the grants do the restricting.
- **Set values stay set (section 6).** The never-cleared trigger refuses to clear or change a set `revoked_at`, `suspect_at` or `used_at`, so every revocation sets `revoked_at` only where it is still null; a check constraint, `staff_keys_suspect_is_revoked`, keeps `suspect_at` from being set without `revoked_at`.
- **`CONSOLE_ORIGIN` is written as a browser sends it (section 8).** Scheme, host and port only: lowercase, no path, no trailing slash, no default port, because the staff gate compares the `Origin` header with it as a string; equality with `APP_ORIGIN` and the `TRUSTED_ORIGINS` entries is judged by origin; production also refuses an IP address or `localhost` for the console, as for the app; a `CONSOLE_RP_ID` set while `CONSOLE_ORIGIN` is unset is kept.
- **The functions' answers (section 6).** `auth.add_staff_key` returns the key's id, `auth.append_audit` the row's `chain_seq`, and `auth.forget_staff_keys` how many keys it blanked; refusals raise the staff error code itself as the message (`staff_enrollment_invalid`, `staff_key_limit`), which the flows map; a `staff_key_added` row's metadata is `{"enrollmentId": ...}`, never the key's name or AAGUID.
- **Contracts the design left open (section 10).** `StaffEnrollVerifyResponse` is `{ key: StaffKey }`, `StaffSignInVerifyResponse` is `StaffMe`, `AuditPageQuery` refuses `cursor` and `at` together, `StaffMe` refuses an idle end later than the absolute end, and `STAFF_AUDIT_PAGE_SIZE` is 50.
- **Grant-role's first statement locks the account (section 7, Role changes).** It is a `SELECT ... FOR NO KEY UPDATE` of the account's row, which takes the same lock as the role's update, because the `role_granted` row needs the previous role, which `UPDATE ... RETURNING` does not give.
- **`audit-verify`'s session settings (section 7, Command line).** It sets `DateStyle` ISO, `TimeZone` UTC and the 10-second `lock_timeout` with `SET LOCAL` at the start of its verifying transaction, so the same check runs inside a transaction a test hands it (`checkAuditRecord(tx, kept, keysFrom)`, whose keys come from the auth role when the handed transaction is on the API's).
- **What `audit-verify` also refuses (section 7).** Rows at a place of 0 or below, rows beyond the head, and kept places that name no row.
- **Each command reads only its own settings (section 7).** `staff.js` never loads the API's configuration: `audit-head` reads `DATABASE_URL_API`, `audit-verify` that and `DATABASE_URL_AUTH`, each through a narrow schema (`staffDatabaseUrls`), so it runs with the console off, moved or misconfigured; `config.ts` exports the PostgreSQL URL rule both use.
- **Bundle entries never import each other (section 5).** In a bundle every module's `import.meta.url` is the bundle's, so an entry that imported another entry's file would run that entry's main too; the lock-timeout helpers live in `cli/lock-timeout.ts`, `SYSTEM_ACTOR_ID` moved to `auth/admin.ts`, and `build.mjs` says so.
- **The gate's answers (section 7, The staff gate).** Another Host gets the app's own unknown-route 404 (`c.notFound()`), compared exactly, without lowercasing; a failed Origin or `Sec-Fetch-Site` test is `AuthError("csrf_failed", 403)`.
- **The reader past the head (section 7, The audit log).** For an `at` beyond the head the reader returns the newest page.
- **Who the take-down's record names (section 7).** The account itself in `takeDown`, since its owner asked for the deletion, and the system actor in `finishTakeDown`, which the purge job runs; `finishTakeDown` now takes the account's row first with `FOR NO KEY UPDATE`, as every writer of staff rows does.
- **The shapes of the staff record's rows (section 7).** `staff_key_revoked`: target `staff_key`, metadata `{ keyId, sessionsRevoked, via }`, `key_id` null; `staff_enrollments_cancelled`: target `user`, metadata `{ count, via }`; an enrolment issued by `staff.js enroll`: target `user`, metadata `{ enrollmentId, via: "cli" }`.
- **The take-down's enrolments (section 7).** It deletes every enrolment, spent ones too, and its `staff_enrollments_cancelled` row counts only the links that were still open, written only when there was one.
- **`staff.js keys` without an email (section 7).** It lists live accounts whose role is not `user`, and reads their handles on the API's role, so it needs both database URLs.
- **The command line's mailer (section 7).** `cli/mail.ts` builds it from `SMTP_URL` and `MAIL_FROM`; grant-role uses it, and its result gains the staff counts and `mailError`.
- **No limit of its own on enrolment (section 7).** The enrolment routes have only the global rate limit; the link's 30 minutes and single use bound them.
- **BS without BE is malformed (section 7, Sign-in).** @simplewebauthn/server 14.0.2 rejects an assertion that reports BS without BE before the flow sees its flags, so that case answers `staff_key_invalid`; BE, backed up or not, answers `staff_key_not_device_bound` as designed.
- **The marked read is an update (section 7, Every staff request).** A request marked `X-Staff-Activity: 1` reads and slides its session in one `UPDATE ... FROM` the staff keys joined to the users; the account is reached as the key's owner, which the sessions' foreign key on `(key_id, user_id)` makes the session's account.
- **An expired sign-in challenge (section 7, Sign-in).** It answers the shared `challenge_expired`, as enrolment does, which section 10 allows; forged, other-purpose and spent challenges answer `staff_key_invalid`.
- **The sign-in record's shapes (section 7).** `staff_sign_in` and `staff_signed_out` rows: the account as actor, the session as target (`staff_session`, its handle), the handle and the key in their columns, metadata `{}`; their auth events carry `{ keyId, handle }` and `{ handle }`; `staff_key_counter_regression`: the key's owner as actor, the key as target, metadata `{ keyId, sessionsRevoked, via }`.
- **What the console reads (section 7, Sessions and keys).** `GET /api/staff/keys` lists live keys only, since `StaffKey` has no revoked field; sign-in options have only the global rate limit.
- **`staff.js revoke`'s edges (section 7, Command line).** An already revoked key exits 0 having written nothing and mailed nothing, and so does `all` with nothing left; an unknown account, or a key that is unknown or another account's, exits 1; it reads `DATABASE_URL_AUTH`, `SMTP_URL`, `MAIL_FROM` and `NODE_ENV` only.
- **The step-up middleware validates the body (section 7, Step-up).** `requireStaffStepUp` validates the action's strict params with an optional `stepUp` through the shared validator, so a missing assertion answers `staff_step_up_required` rather than `invalid_request`; the route reads the confirmed result from `staffStepUp`.
- **Status codes (sections 7 and 10).** `staff_step_up_required` and `staff_step_up_invalid` answer 403; a handle that names no live session of the person's own answers `404 not_found` ("No such session"), as the app's own session revocation does.
- **The re-check before the action (section 7, Step-up).** The revocation's transaction locks the account's row, then checks that the confirming key and the account are still live, answering `staff_session_required` and writing nothing otherwise; a person may revoke the session they confirm from.
- **Lower-case targets (section 10).** A step-up target id is PostgreSQL's lower-case uuid only (`LowerCaseUuid`); any other spelling is refused with `invalid_request`, because the record hashes the target exactly as confirmed and stores the database's form.
- **`staff_session_required` clears the cookies wherever it is raised (section 7).** `requireStaff` checks `c.error` after `next()`, since Hono hands an error thrown behind it to `app.onError`, and clears both staff cookies on the answer.
- **A step-up challenge needs a minute left (section 7, Step-up).** It carries the full 10 minutes, but is read only while more than one minute is left (`STEP_UP_READ_MARGIN_MS`), so a confirmed row is never written after the expiry `audit-verify` checks; the margin assumes the API's and the database's clocks agree.
- **What `audit-verify` also checks (section 7).** That the stored `action_hash` equals the recomputed one, and it reports a challenge used twice as its own problem; it does not check `metadata.params` against the action's schema.
- **The console's type declarations (section 9).** There is no `@types/react-dom` in the lockfile, so `src/react-dom.d.ts` declares `react-dom/client` and `react-dom/server`, as the app's tests do; `@types/react` 19.2.18 and `@types/node` 24.13.5, both already locked, are its devDependencies.
- **"Your staff session ended" (section 9).** It shows when the page held a session, or when the refused request carried the staff CSRF cookie (read before sending, since the 401 clears it), so a reload or a new tab after an idle end says so too; a 401 with neither (never signed in, signed out, past the cookie's 12 hours) shows plain sign-in.
- **The home screen's 7 days (section 9).** Opening Home does one marked `GET /api/staff/me` and counts the 7 days back from that answer's server time, not from the session read at sign-in.
- **The console's own checks (section 9).** The step-up check also checks the challenge's version byte, and every ceremony forces user verification "required", attestation "none" and no extension but `credProps`, whatever the server's options say; the staff CSRF header goes on every request while the cookie exists.
- **The console site's headers live in `apps/admin/site-headers.mjs` (sections 8 and 9).** The development server uses them; Task 7's Caddyfile and the scan that compares them must match.
- **The app's site refuses staff paths with two handles (section 8).** Caddy 2.11.4 sorts `handle` blocks by their path's length and compares paths only when a handle matches exactly one, so one handle matching both `/api/staff` and `/api/staff/*` is not reliably placed ahead of `handle /api/*`; two one-path handles, longer than `/api/*`, always are. The refusal is a shared snippet that answers the API's error envelope without a request id, which is how the smoke test tells Caddy's answer from the API's.
- **`immutable` only on real build files (section 8).** The console site's hashed-file rule adds Caddy's `file` condition to `path /assets/*`, so the `index.html` fallback served for a missing hashed name keeps `no-store, no-transform`.
- **The browser check's reach (section 12).** Beyond the screens section 12 lists, it covers an unknown address, sign-out and the enrolment refusal of a synced passkey; CI runs it with `KORBAT_BROWSER_CHANNEL=chrome`.
- **Every ceremony's challenge is checked before the key is asked (sections 5, 9 and 11; found by the review).** The contracts export the 58-byte layout (`CEREMONY_CHALLENGE`) and every purpose code (`CHALLENGE_PURPOSES`) beside `STAFF_STEP_UP_CHALLENGE`, and the codec reads them from there. Before every `navigator.credentials` call the console checks the challenge: at sign-in 58 bytes, version 1, purpose `staff_signin` and a zero binding; at enrolment 58 bytes, version 1, purpose `staff_register` (its binding names the enrolment, which the page is never told, so it cannot be checked there); at step-up the 74-byte check. No key is asked at sign-in or enrolment to sign another ceremony's challenge.
- **`audit-verify` reads every row (section 7, Command line; found by the review).** It pages on `(chain_seq, id)` and, in the same snapshot, fails on a place held by two rows, a row with no place, or a row count that does not equal the rows read plus the rows beyond the head.
- **Keys are judged by where they were enrolled (sections 2 and 7; found by the review).** A key whose recorded origin or relying party ID differs from the running configuration is `staff_key_invalid` at sign-in, before the signature, and `staff_step_up_invalid` at the step-up's options and confirmation; assertions are verified against the key's recorded values. Moving the console means enrolling every key again, and the API enforces it.
- **The enrolment page signs in with the new key itself (sections 2 and 9; found by the review).** Its "Sign in with this key" button narrows the allowed credentials to the key just registered and signs in whatever session the browser holds, so the check after each enrolment always uses the new key.
- **A confirmed action never lands after its expiry (sections 2 and 7; found by the review).** The confirmed revocation's transaction sets `lock_timeout` to the lesser of 15 seconds and a third of the challenge's remaining life by the database's clock, and the statement that writes its audit row reads the database's clock after the insert and undoes everything when the challenge has expired; a late confirmation writes nothing and answers `challenge_expired`. The one-minute read margin no longer assumes the API's and the database's clocks agree.
- **`auth.forget_staff_keys` blanks only revoked keys (section 6; found by the review).** Migration 0013 restates it so it blanks the name, AAGUID and transports only of keys whose `revoked_at` is set, of an account marked deleted; the take-down revokes them earlier in the same transaction, and code in the API gains nothing it cannot already do by revoking.
- **Revocation order and grant-role's after-commit steps (section 7, Role changes; found by the review).** Demotion and take-down revoke keys before staff sessions, as `staff.js revoke` does, so a concurrent sign-in cannot keep an unrevoked session; grant-role's cache tombstones and its mail run as independent best-effort steps after the commit, each reported as a warning, and the command exits 0 once the change is committed.
- **Smaller fixes (sections 7 and 9; found by the review).** `staff.js keys` reads in read-only transactions with a 10-second lock timeout; the console reads a marked `/me` right before the step-up options and every `/me` answer replaces the page's session; Go to place says when there is no row at the place asked for; an older Load older's answer never joins a page opened after it; the browser check's fixtures answer with the API's own statuses.

## 16. Changed by 3c (2026-10-09)

`docs/superpowers/specs/2026-10-02-moderation-cases-3c-design.md` (moderation cases) is the first work to stand on this foundation. It adds three step-up actions beside `staff_session_revoked` (`case_decided`, `appeals_reviewed` and `identity_revealed`, each a confirmed row that names its decision or its item), the console's queue, case page, composer and appeals, six commands of `staff.js` (`link`, `unlink`, `limits`, `text-verify`, `account-facts` and `access-request`), and staff mails that go to every staff account. What it changes in this document:

- **Three exceptions to the step-up rule (section 2, Confirming an action).** "A route that changes something asks for a fresh assertion" now has three named exceptions beside enrolment, sign-in, the step-up's own options and sign-out: saving a text (`POST /api/staff/cases/:case/texts`), taking a fresh snapshot (`POST /api/staff/cases/:case/snapshots`) and opening a finding (`POST /api/staff/findings`). None restricts or releases anything: a text enters the record only when a confirmed decision or reveal names its salted digest, and a finding is limited per staff account and day and counted on the home screen. The route-table test lists every changing route without a step-up by method and path.
- **"Followed only by deferred checks that read" (sections 6 and 7).** The rule that an audit row is always the last statement of its transaction becomes: followed only by deferred checks that read. A decision's audit row is written last by `append_confirmed_audit`, and at COMMIT the database's deferred constraint triggers hold the decision and every row of its ledger against that audit row; they take only ACCESS SHARE locks, which `korbat_api` cannot block, so the head's lock is still never held across a wait.
- **`ConsolePath` (section 9).** It becomes `"/" | "/audit" | "/signin" | "/queue" | "/appeals"`. The console gains one more address built from a value, a case's (`caseHref` over a `CaseId` that only `parseCaseId` makes, a lower-case uuid), written by `CaseLink` in `src/nav.tsx`, and one image site, `src/media.tsx`, whose address is built from two checked ids and a literal size; the source test pins both. Images reach the console only from its own origin, under the policy of section 8 unchanged.
- **The staff answers' new shapes (section 10).** The staff API gains the overview, the queue, a case, its images, snapshots and texts, the decision, the appeals and the review, and the reveal. No member of any answer is named like `email`, `address`, `userId`, `accountId` or `actorId`: people are handles, and a report's source is a summary in bands until a confirmed reveal. The route-table test's walk runs over the new answers and fails on a schema kind it does not read, and no staff route answers HEAD. The browser check gains the new screens with hostile fixtures, and the statuses a console request may meet gain 422 and 429.
- **`korbat_auth` can no longer clear or back-date `auth.users.deleted_at` (section 6, and the amendment on `auth.forget_staff_keys` in section 15).** Migration 0018's trigger `users_deleted_mark` makes a mark that `korbat_auth` sets the transaction's `now()` and refuses to clear or change one that is set. So the note in migration 0013 that `korbat_auth` may set and clear the mark is superseded; `auth.forget_staff_keys` still blanks only revoked keys.
- **The record (sections 6 and 7).** `staff.js audit-verify` is unchanged; `case_decided`, `appeals_reviewed` and `identity_revealed` are step-up actions, so it refuses a row of them without a valid assertion, and the pinned "nested metadata" vector of this design's tests, a `case_decided` row with no step-up, is now reported with two problems. `staff.js keys` prints, after each account's keys, how many personal accounts are linked to it, never which. The README's staff steps after a restore, which this design's documentation task wrote (section 13), gain a fifth, Moderation.

## 17. Changed by 3f (2026-10-17)

`docs/superpowers/specs/2026-10-09-authorities-orders-3f-design.md` changes the step-up's actions, the console's width and routes, the staff mails and the console's site.

- **Section 10:** `STAFF_STEP_UP_ACTIONS` gains `order_effected`, `order_event_recorded`, `order_corrected`, `audit_exported` and `gap_closed`; `case_decided`'s action entry gains `reinstate_by_order` with `orderGround`. The keeper's daily visit stays: only the keeper holds the place.
- **Section 4** ("publishing the audit head ... (3d)"): done here.

# korbat sub-project 3c: moderation cases

Date: 2026-10-03. Status: draft r8, written without the user under the standing instruction of 2026-09-23 (keep going; leave only account-dependent steps). The architecture pass restructured draft r4 by nine accepted simplification proposals, P1 to P9, each applied with the conditions its three judges set (`korbat-scratch/research-3c/simplify-r5.md` records them, their votes and what was removed or moved): restriction state is derived from a ledger of measures (P1); every restricting answer owns its measures (P2); deletion and moderation write disjoint columns (P3); suspicion of child sexual abuse material follows the material (P4); appeals have one shape, the author's, and notifiers get re-examination (P5); authorities' orders (P6) and strikes with handle retirement (P7) move to 3e; retention waits only for each kind of data's own users (P8); and each rule is stated once (P9). The decisions in section 2 were taken here and are flagged for review. Research: `korbat-scratch/research-3c/` (`repo-3c.md`, a map of the code after 3a; `law-3c.md`, the law with its obligations table; `practice-3c.md`, how working systems moderate; `threats-3c.md`, threats T39 to T62 and controls C1 to C40; ten gap answers `gap-G1.md` to `gap-G10.md`, each with lab measurements on PostgreSQL 18.6; and the review records `review-r1.md` to `review-r6.md`), and the earlier `korbat-scratch/research-3/{practice,threats}.md`. This design splits the 3c scope of the main design's amendment of 2026-10-01 into two designs (section 2, first row). This one, 3c, is designed in full: notices and reports, cases, decisions with statements of reasons on posts, images and profile fields, evidence, the author's appeal, the notifier's and reporter's re-examination, the author's and the notifier's screens and mails, the console's case screens, the export and the terms. ## 1. Context

3a gave staff a console of their own, keys that open it, a step-up that confirms each action with the session's own key, and an audit log that is a hash chain. It gave them nothing to moderate. The trust-and-safety tables of migration 0000 (`cases`, `reports`, `appeals`, `strikes`, `transparency_log`, `packages/db/src/schema/safety.ts:11-96`) have no reader or writer in any app (`repo-3c.md` section 1.7), and they cannot hold what the law now asks: a `reports` row needs a reporter and a rule (`safety.ts:36,39`), so a notice from someone without an account, or about content illegal under a national law but outside R1 to R6, has nowhere to go (Digital Services Act Art. 16, `law-3c.md` section 1). Nothing in the code sets `withheld` or `removed`; every read already honours them (`repo-3c.md` section 2). An author can delete a withheld or removed post and its images today, and an account deletion blanks every post and deletes every image (`apps/api/src/social/repo.ts:480-497,1079-1121`), so the evidence of a case would vanish before anyone decided it.

korbat's promise is that content limits are narrow and public, that every removal cites a public rule, shows the author exactly what happened and can be appealed to a different human, and that there is no silent reach reduction (main design, Context). 3c is where that promise is built or broken. It must also meet the law that binds a micro platform now: Art. 16 notices from anyone, Art. 17 statements of reasons for every restriction, Art. 14 terms that describe the procedure, the TCO Regulation's terrorist-content policy in the terms (`law-3c.md` key findings 1 to 4, 8), Art. 18 and TCO Art. 14(5), which oblige korbat to tell the authorities promptly when it learns of a suspected offence threatening someone's life or safety (met in 3c by the runbook and `staff.js account-facts`; 3e records the notifications, `law-3c.md` 3), and the GDPR for notifiers, reporters and the people reported. And it must not give one or two tired moderators, or someone who stole their key, more power than the record can account for (`threats-3c.md` sections 3.4 and 6).

This design delivers: an intake that takes reports from signed-in users and Art. 16 notices from anyone into one model of intakes and items, merged into one open case per target as a database fact; a queue ordered by severity and age, with no weighting; decisions on posts, single images and profile fields, each carrying a statement of reasons whose every Art. 17(3) element is data, confirmed by the deciding person's staff key without any free text entering the chain; a ledger of measures from which every post's and image's restriction is derived by the database; evidence copied or held at the first report and protected from every destructive path; the author's appeal of a final restriction, reviewed by a different person, which the database enforces, and re-examination of "no action" for notifiers and reporters; the console's queue, case and appeal screens; the app's report form, notice status page and case screens; the mails; the export's moderation section; and the moderation parts of the draft terms and the rulebook.

| Queue order and weight | Nothing is weighted. Reporter standing, report counts and the badge are never keys (G9 3.8: weighting by standing makes the legal path slower for strangers by design, rewards aged brigades, and practice that works without auto-hiding orders by severity). A published emergency switch (`MODERATION_DEFER_UNPROVEN`) sorts cases whose open items all come from unproven sources after the others of their lane, never below a less severe lane, and in lane 0 only signed-out intakes count as unproven, so a new account reporting a threat against itself is never deferred (7.3). 3c drops `profiles.reputation`; write limits stay on account age (`apps/api/src/social/tiers.ts`), and nothing a decision records feeds a limit or a weight (T53, C28). Staff see a reporter as a summary computed on read, never a stored score, in bands, never exact counts, because the summary is the same on every case the person reported and must rarely single them out across cases (7.3). | Case targets and measures | Two target kinds: a **post** and an **account** (its profile fields; in 3e, its standing); one image is a scope inside a post case, so a report about an image and one about the text merge (G3 key finding 1). Measures: on a post, `withhold` (interim only) and `remove`; on the images a case reaches, `seal_media` (while deciding or for good, on a post case or an account case; 6.2); on one image, `withhold_media` (interim only) and `remove_media`; on an account, `reset_display_name` and `reset_bio`; each a row of the ledger, and each reversal a row naming exactly one measure (6.1 `action_kind`, 6.2). A decision may hold several measures with one statement (TDB's own example combines four kinds, G3 3), at most one of them a post measure. **Every restricting answer owns its measures** (P2): a final decision that finds a breach records `restricted` with measures of its own, whatever the target's level or lifecycle (a removal of a post already removed or deleted, a second seal, an interim withhold of a post not visible); each stays in force on its own should another be reversed, and its statement, the notifiers' line and the console say when it changed nothing anyone sees now (`no_effect`, 6.2). No outcome closes an item by pointing at another case: a final decision answers `restricted`, `no_violation` or `not_evident`, and `not_available` is only the automatic answer to a link that names nothing live (7.1 step 3). A field reset writes its placeholder once, at its decision, and holds nothing afterwards. Its author may set the field again at any time. What they set is their own edit: it is judged on its own when someone reports it (the report takes a new snapshot of the account, 7.1 step 4), and a new decision resets it again, while deciding too (6.2 step 5). Holding a field against its author's edits would be a partial suspension of the service, which korbat imposes only as a measure with a statement of its own: 3e's narrower restrictions (G3 7.1). Flagged (owner): until 3e an author can set a reset field again at once, and only a new decision resets it again. Flagged: one image or one field instead of the post or the account is the least restrictive measure the model makes possible (Art. 14(4)); it costs `post_media.moderation_state` and a placeholder for others. Flagged (owner): an author may now receive several statements about one post that draws reports over time, and a moderator judges every later report about a removed or deleted post on its merits. A notice or report naming an account is answered for its display name and bio, and its notifier reads `ACCOUNT_ITEM_SCOPE` with the outcome (section 10). What the account's posts and images showed is decided in cases of their own. A notice or report naming a post that quotes another is answered for that post's own text and images, and its notifier reads `QUOTE_ITEM_SCOPE` with the outcome (section 10). The quoted post its card shows is decided in a case of its own. Flagged for counsel: a notifier who named an account, or a post whose card showed the post it quotes, is not told what korbat's own findings decided about the account's posts or the quoted post. On the path for child sexual abuse material both differ (6.1, the freeze): a suspect item about an account is answered in a case that reaches every image on the account's posts, and its notifier reads `ACCOUNT_SUSPECT_SCOPE` with the outcome, as does the sender of any other item about the account that a decision holding `seal_media` answers, since that answer does concern the images on the account's posts; a suspect item about a post that quotes another brings an item on the quoted post, so its notifier reads an answer about each post and no `QUOTE_ITEM_SCOPE`. Flagged for counsel: on that path a notifier who named an account is not told what korbat decided, in cases of their own, about single posts of the account or about what its posts say (Art. 16(5)). | A target kind per image (two cases for one post); detaching a removed image (the sweeper deletes unattached uploads, `apps/api/src/media/repo.ts:157-160`); a hidden-field state on profiles (G3 7.1); r4's outcomes "Already restricted" and a moderator's "Not available", which closed items on a measure the case did not own, so another case's reversal republished content an order, a notice or an admin's R5 judgment concerned, and which needed refusal lists keyed on grounds (r3-8, r4-4, r4-5; class C2); strikes and handle retirement in 3c (row Splitting 3c). |
| Decisions and statements | A decision is the statement of reasons: every Art. 17(3) element is a column (the measures and their durations, the territorial scope, the facts, the source, automation, the legal or contractual ground with its explanation, the redress), in the Transparency Database's shape (`decision_ground`, `category`, `source_type`, the automated flags, a random `puid`) without personal data in any enumerated field, so 3d can publish it (`law-3c.md` 7.3; 6.1). The rulebook is versioned (`RULES_VERSION` 2; version 1 kept) and every decision records the rules and redress versions it was made under, so an old statement renders exactly as sent (practice-3c 11.4); one pure function, `statementParagraphs`, renders it for the author's screen, the console's preview and the mail, so what the moderator previews is what the author gets (practice-3c 10.4; section 10). The statement names the source category only, never a count, a reporter or a report's words (T47). `REDRESS_VERSION` 1 holds three texts: korbat's appeal, for a final restriction; the interim text, for a decision taken while deciding; and the text for a decision its author cannot appeal (section 10); 3e adds an order's. The author is told, in the app at once and by mail, of every decision that restricts, reverses, or ends or lifts a measure taken while deciding, and of every review (6.2 step 10); an interim measure on a target already deleted, which can never take effect, is recorded without a mail. Flagged: telling authors of no-action decisions (T46 suggests it for legal-ground notices) was not adopted, because it would tell them that someone reported them. Flagged: worldwide scope is more restrictive than a single state's law requires, and the statement says so. | Free text under the step-up | G1's option (a), "draft first, then confirm". Three writing staff routes therefore stand without a step-up, by name: saving a text, taking a fresh snapshot, and opening a case on the moderator's own finding; none changes anything a user sees (a saved `seal_declined` text ends an urgent repeat and is listed on the home screen, 7.12), and each enters the record only through a confirmed decision that names its digest or its case. One migrator-owned function, `moderation_apply`, is the only writer of the moderation columns: under the post's lock it takes the strongest measure in force over every case, and under the image rows' locks each image's state (6.2). The result does not depend on the order in which cases, measures and reversals arrive, no case's effect reasons about another's, a new kind of measure only joins the maximum, and an auditor can recompute it (`staff.js text-verify` does). No reversal writes content. A plain trigger on `posts` and column grants keep every other writer off (6.1). Flagged (owner): a lifted or ended field reset does not give the old value back. A lift after the copy was erased (a correction after the restriction became final, or after an R4 redaction of the account) finds none, and its statement then makes no such promise (section 10). Keeping the resetting decision's snapshot for as long as a final reset stands was not adopted: it would keep content found to break a rule, for a lift that may never come (GDPR 5(1)(c), (e); P8). | Lock order | One order for every transaction that touches moderation: profile rows first (sorted by id, each in the strongest mode the transaction will need), then cases (in their targets' order), then, inside a decision's triggers, the deciding account's and the subject's `auth.users` rows `FOR SHARE` and the cap's advisory lock, then the case's own post, then image rows in id order, then inserts, the audit row and the deferred checks (6.2). An intake takes its cases in their targets' order, then its post targets `FOR SHARE` in id order, then every image row it reaches in one global id order `FOR KEY SHARE` (7.1); it never locks a post it reaches only through an account. The R4 redaction takes the case, then the post, then the post's images in id order (6.4). A seal takes image rows only, in id order; no decision locks a post other than its own case's (6.2). The author's deletion and the purge delete image rows in id order, as `dropDisposable` does (7.10), so nothing locks image rows in another order than an intake that reaches them through an account, which takes no lock on their posts. Flagged: the account purge still updates posts before other accounts' profiles (G5 4.3); a decision that meets it rarely deadlocks, and the decision's one retry covers it. Flagged (owner): measured under load (section 3, lab `lab-gate-k`), the purge of an account with 5,000 image rows takes 2 to 4 s and with 20,000 rows 7 to 16 s, the keep trigger reading the freeze once for each row, and an account's seal takes 1.5 s at 5,000 image rows and 5.9 s at 20,000. The same check on the case's subject refuses opening a case, its images, snapshots and texts, and every reveal in it, and it does not look at reporters, so a refused read says nothing about who reported (6.2 `staff_case_conflict`; 7.3). No final decision may restrict a staff account (`staff_target`, G5 6): staff are disciplined by demotion through grant-role, while an interim measure applies to them as to anyone, so a threat posted from a staff account stops being public at once, and images on a staff account's posts that are reported as child sexual abuse material can be sealed while deciding. Flagged (owner): "senior" becomes "admin"; with one admin, final R2 and R5 decisions and every answer to a suspect item wait for them. Flagged (owner): the first seal is taken while deciding, by any moderator, on a report nobody can check, and hides the images from their author too (r7 showed a post withheld while deciding to its author). The owner may choose r7's form, in which the author loses sight only when an admin seals for good; korbat then serves a file reported as child sexual abuse material to its uploader for as long as the admin is away. Flagged (owner): one moderator's decision while deciding seals every image of an account, also on a finding that moderator opened, and only an admin lifts it. In r7 such a decision hid one post. Flagged (owner): reviews inheriting every `needs_admin` (R5 included) was proposed and not adopted, because with one admin those appeals would wait for good (T60); the owner may choose it. Flagged: no "obvious case" exception for a recused moderator (practice-3c 10.20 allows one with a recorded justification); with one moderator the case waits. | Evidence | Text by copy, images by reference (G6). The first report, notice or finding on a target, and every fresh snapshot, copies the post's or profile's content into an append-only snapshot with a server-made salt and digest, under the post's `FOR SHARE` lock, so an author's deletion comes after it or leaves a tombstone the copy records (G6 E3c); a capture of erased content copies none of it (6.1, T52). Images are held on their own row, which every delete path skips (G6 E3 to E5b); the images and the snapshots of a frozen post are kept by two gates of their own, whatever case holds them and whether a hold stands or not (6.1, the freeze; the keep trigger measured on PostgreSQL 18.6, section 3); one disposal predicate deletes what nothing retains (7.9). The decision names the snapshot and the digest the console computed from what it displayed (T52). Retention follows each kind of data's own users (P8, 6.4, 6.6). Flagged: the snapshot's digest enters the chain only with the decision that names it, not at capture (an intake by anyone would otherwise write a chained row, and an API compromised before the report can forge consistently anyway). Flagged (owner): snapshots of a no-action case go about a day after it closes instead of six months after the notifiers' release (a privacy gain, published in the terms), so a re-examination judges the target as it then stands, and an intake's texts may outlive their case's snapshots by up to six months and 30 days. Flagged (owner): a report or finding of child sexual abuse material, a false one included, keeps every image its case reaches that its author deletes meanwhile, those of a purged account included, unserved, until an admin answers (T41). Flagged: a suspect item about an account copies the account's fields, not its posts' texts. Flagged (owner): others see "Image hidden by korbat moderation" on each sealed image of a post that stays public; after an account's seal that is every image post of the profile. r7's withhold while deciding took the post out of others' sight without a mark. | Suspected child sexual abuse material | Nobody at korbat opens it. The mechanics are stated once, in 6.1 (the freeze) and 6.2 (the seal); this row gives the decision and its flags. A report on the CSAM path, or a moderator's finding citing R2, is a **suspect item**. While it is unanswered, every post its case reaches is **frozen**: a post case reaches its post, an account case every post of the account, and a report about a post that quotes another is taken in as two items, one for each post, so no case reaches another author's post. Frozen means three things, each enforced at one gate that every path of its kind must pass: no image row of the post is deleted and no file of it requested (a trigger), no snapshot of it is erased (the one function that erases snapshots), and no staff member is served its images, on any case, open or closed (the one function that opens an image for staff). A report hides nothing by itself. A person does, with one measure, the **seal**: it seals every image the case reaches, for everyone, their author included; whoever is on duty takes it while deciding, and an admin takes it for good or answers without it. Only images are sealed, never text. Every suspect item about something that exists waits for an admin, who answers all suspect items of a case at once, and only an admin lifts a seal, a seal for good only on the answer of the authority the images were reported to (6.2, the seal; 7.7). On a seal for good the operator reports to the national police or the authority its Member State names, never to a hotline, whose analyst assesses what an address shows while a sealed image answers 404 to everyone (`research-3/practice.md` INHOPE paragraph), and an admin seals for good only what korbat then reports (runbook, Task 12(a)). Every staff account is mailed at once after a decision that lifts a seal or answers a suspect item without one, and the home screen lists them for 30 days, as for reveals (7.5 step 4, 7.12). 3c keeps what it sealed: the release, the quarantine and the replay after a restore are 3d's, and the record of the report to the authority is 3e's (sections 16, 17). Flagged (owner): a report of child sexual abuse material hides nothing by itself. From the report until a staff member seals the images while deciding they stay public: for as long as it takes one of one or two people to read a mail, hours at night, a day or more when both are away. The urgent mail, repeated about every 20 minutes, is the only alert until 3e's phone alert, and lane 0's target is 24 hours. After a seal, Cloudflare's edge and browsers may still serve a copy for up to five minutes, until 3d's purge. Until the seal only the rule that staff never open a reported post in the app keeps them from seeing it, and after it the app still shows what the case does not reach. The person who seals cannot look: here "a person decides" means that a person may refuse, in a flood or on a plain repeat, and acts under a name, a key, a record and the caps. What shrinks the window without a program deciding on a report is 3e's phone alert and 3d's hash match, both before sub-project 4. Flagged (owner): the seal on an account case covers every image on the account's posts, because nobody can tell which ones the report means. So one anonymous report that names an account, and that nobody can check, can hide every image the account ever posted from everyone, its author included; the report form asks for the post or the image instead where the sender can give it (section 9). An admin who can tell from the report's words which post is meant opens a finding on that post instead and answers the account's item without a seal. The account's notifier then reads its answer with `ACCOUNT_SUSPECT_SCOPE`, and the statement of the finding's seal names a moderator's finding as its source. Flagged for counsel: whether Art. 17(3)(b) needs that statement to say that it followed a notice. Flagged (owner): a seal covers the images that exist when it is taken. Until 3e's suspension an account whose images are sealed can post new ones; while its item is unanswered they are frozen and the urgent mail starts again, after a recorded choice not to seal as after a seal (7.12), and after the answer they need a report of their own. Flagged (owner): a report of this kind about a post that quotes another opens a case on the quoted post too, in the urgent lane, so that author's images are frozen, and may be sealed, on a report that named someone else's post; the notifier may have meant the quoting post's own images. An added item does not count against a notice's ten targets, so a notice of ten quoting posts opens twenty urgent cases. Flagged (owner): after an admin's answer without a seal, moderators may open the images (as round 2 decision 21 allowed for a closed case), and every staff account is mailed. That answer is, in effect, the decision that staff may now look: the first person who opens an image afterwards is the first to learn what it is. Flagged (owner): 3c's software has no function to release, hand over or erase sealed images; it keeps them, and the operator does either by hand on an authority's written instruction (runbook). korbat does not meet people the operator does not know before 3e and 3d have shipped (row Splitting 3c). A restore before then loses every freeze and seal recorded after the backup: sealed images are back as public as they were at the backup until a staff key is enrolled again and an admin seals again, and the retention switch is what keeps the job from deleting them meanwhile (README, Restoring). Flagged (owner): a false report can get every image of an account sealed until the authority answers, which no law obliges it to do. An admin's seal for good is taken without anyone having seen the images; korbat then reports the author to the police with what it holds about the account, the author's appeal waits without a time limit, and 3c has no release. The admin's other answer, without a seal, is as unseen, and after it staff may open the images. Flagged (owner): a report of this kind, a false one included, takes the images of every post its case reaches out of staff's sight on every case until an admin answers. Reports on other grounds about those images, corrections and the author's appeals are meanwhile decided on text alone or wait; an admin's answer also answers the earlier reports of its case unseen (their senders are told so and may ask again); and whoever sends a new report after each answer, the author of the post included, keeps it so, at five notices an hour from one network. What breaks the loop is a person: staff open the images after an answer without a seal, and the next answer carries the measure for what they saw (6.1, the freeze; 7.5 step 1; runbook, Task 12(a)). Flagged (owner): the statement of a seal tells its author of the report at once, and Art. 17 gives korbat no right to delay it; an author who then deletes the account takes with it the address korbat could have given the police. So whoever has the server runs `staff.js account-facts` as soon as the urgent mail arrives and keeps its output off the server until the admin's answer (runbook); the seal never waits for it. Whether an account under a seal can be deleted before the report is made is 3e's to decide (section 16). Flagged (owner): a report of this kind about an account reaches neither the posts it reposted nor the posts its posts quote, though its profile shows their images; and one about a post reaches neither the post it replies to nor its replies, though the post's page in the app shows them with their images. So staff never open a post or an account in the app while a suspect item about it is unanswered or its images are sealed (6.1, the freeze), and an admin who can tell from the report's words that such a post is meant opens a finding on it. Flagged: after an answer without a seal the case page shows, for a post, the day staff last opened one of its images in the console (7.3, `imagesOpenedOn`); nothing on the server but a note records a look at an account's images in the app, and a note goes with its case's evidence (6.4; runbook). Flagged: a delete that fired before a suspect item was committed, on a row the intake could not lock, wins: the report then came too late for that image, as it would have a moment later. Flagged: a stream of suspect items into one case can keep an admin from answering it; that fails closed, and an admin can still lift a wrong seal taken while deciding by a correction (6.2, `decisions_record` step 6). Flagged: a suspect item that was answered by a measure on text without a seal cannot be re-examined, and when the item korbat added for a quoted post is closed to re-examination, a re-examination of the quoting post's item freezes that post alone; the notifier's way to bring the quoted post's images before an admin again is a new notice (7.2). Flagged for counsel: whether leaving reported images public until a staff member acts is expeditious under DSA Art. 6(1)(b) for a provider that does not open the material; whether a statement of reasons that says the images were reported as child sexual abuse material and that korbat's staff do not open such images meets Art. 17(3)(b) and (d) or (e); that no provision lets korbat delay that statement, though it tells a suspect of the report before the police act (`research-3/practice.md` 2.3); whether Art. 18(1)'s "promptly" runs from the first seal, taken while deciding, or from the admin's answer; whether a notice that nobody at korbat examined is information giving rise to a suspicion under Art. 18(1), and whether giving the author's data to the police on it is covered by GDPR Art. 6(1)(c); and whether a decision on a notice taken without examining the content, either way, is diligent and objective under Art. 16(6). Flagged for counsel: whether sealing every image of an account on a notice that names the account is proportionate (Art. 14(4)), and whether a seal taken while deciding that an admin does not answer for days is. Flagged for counsel: the statement to the author of a quoted post says that the decision followed a notice and that no automated means were used; the notice named the quoting post, and korbat's software added the item (Art. 17(3)(b) and (c)). Flagged for counsel: `intake_items.suspect`, `decisions.suspect`, `decisions.unseen`, `seal_posts` and the counts of earlier answers are records of a suspected offence about a person, and decisions are kept for good as rows (GDPR Art. 10). Flagged for counsel: what the home Member State's law adds: a duty to report, a rule against telling the suspect, and what "without right" (Directive 2011/93/EU Art. 5(1), recital 17) gives a host that keeps the files for the police. The owner may still choose otherwise, each at its cost. (a) Hiding the images from the report on: it closes the window, and costs an automated decision and statement on one anonymous report nobody checked, against main design lines 172, 180 and 184, with GDPR Art. 22 to answer, and it makes the anonymous path a switch by which anyone hides any account's images until an admin is back, again after every answer without a seal; 3d's hash match seals automatically in any case. (b) r7's form, in which the author keeps seeing the images until an admin seals for good: it keeps main design line 190 whole, and has korbat serve a file reported as child sexual abuse material to its uploader for as long as the admin is away. (c) A timed seal: when nobody has sealed, or recorded a choice not to, within a published number of hours, the database seals while deciding by an automated decision whose statement says so; it bends "a moderator decides" only where no moderator came, and its abuse is (a)'s, delayed. (d) A guard for staff in the app: a session whose role is not `user` gets a placeholder for every image in every view, so that a staff member signed in as staff cannot be shown a reported image there; it costs a rule in the view builder and does nothing for staff who browse signed out. | Viewing it behind a step-up (possession, and the harm to the one or two people who would see it daily, T41); sealing automatically on report volume (main design line 180 forbids it); suspicion computed from which cases ever held which items, and a seal that moved the body out, flagged every snapshot of the post, held images with seal holds and copied the body back on reversal (each new path to the same material needed a rule of its own: r2-19, r2-21, r2-22, r3-27, r3-28, r4-2; class C3); r7's model, in which suspicion was computed from open cases through three joins while holds were rows written at intake for the images that existed then, so that the two sets differed on account targets, quoting posts, deletions, the purge, retention and the redaction, and the seal existed only on a post case (r5-1 to r5-4, r6-1 to r6-8; `korbat-scratch/research-3c/csam-r8.md`); a mark written to each reached image at intake (a second copy of the truth, written to thousands of rows by an anonymous request and unwound row by row); the quoted post as a branch of the predicate (a seal on the quoting post's case would restrict another author's post under a decision about someone else); refusing account targets on this path (an anonymous notifier does not come back, and Art. 16(6) has every notice processed); a seal that hid text (row What the author sees of removed content). |

A notifier's address is never revealed. A review answers that one appeal (`kept`, `partly_reversed`, `reversed`), never restricts and never adds a measure; the database refuses a review by anyone who decided in the case, opened a finding in it, or is a party (C30); with one moderator, appeals wait, and the author's screen says so and why (T60, fail closed; 6.3, 7.7). Interim decisions are not appealable: their measures end with the case's final decision, which can be appealed if it restricts, and anyone eligible may lift one early, except a seal (row Recusal). Notifiers and signed-in reporters get **re-examination**: within six months of the release of an item a moderator answered `no_violation` or `not_evident`, they may ask once, with an optional statement, and the request becomes a new item of the same intake on the same target, decided and told like any item (7.2); an item korbat added for a quoted post is re-examined like any other, and an answer given while nobody could open the post's images (`UNSEEN_NO_ACTION`, section 10) does not spend the one request: it can be asked again, also when it answered a re-examination. Art. 20 does not bind korbat (Art. 19(1); `law-3c.md` final table: NOT BINDING, ADOPT); recital 58's aim, a free, electronic, human re-look at "no action" within six months, is kept, and Art. 16(5)'s redress information names re-examination, the courts and the Digital Services Coordinator. Flagged: korbat cannot keep the "different human" promise with one moderator; the appeal waits without a time limit. Flagged: recital 58's "not adequate" is met for "no action" only. ## 3. Research (facts the design depends on)

- **The code after 3a** (`repo-3c.md`, checked against the files cited here). The five trust-and-safety tables are unchanged since 0000 and unused; `reports.reporter_id` and `rule_id` are NOT NULL (`packages/db/src/schema/safety.ts:36,39`); `reports_reporter_target_idx` is unique for ever (`:48`), so a reporter could never report a target again after its case closed (G3 L14); `cases_target_idx` is neither unique nor partial (`:29`); every one of them is allow-all for `korbat_api` with the default UPDATE and DELETE grants (`:29,50,67,79,95`; `0001_grants.sql:16`). `audit_log` has exactly one index, the unique `chain_seq` one, pinned by `packages/db/test/schema.test.ts:488`. `appendAuditRow` (`apps/api/src/staff/audit.ts:43-60`) is the staff module's writer for public tables, unused by 3a; the late-confirmation guard (`boundLockWaits`, `appendAuditBefore`, `LateConfirmation`) is private to the auth repository (`apps/api/src/auth/repo.ts:1487-1538`) and runs on the auth pool. `requireStaffStepUp` treats the whole body but `stepUp` as the action's params, validated by the action's strict schema (`apps/api/src/auth/staff/step-up.ts:158-178`), and `audit-verify` fails for good any row of a step-up action without a valid assertion, whatever its actor (`apps/api/src/cli/staff.ts:332-334`), and any row stamped at or after its challenge's expiry (`:373`). `STAFF_STEP_UP_ACTIONS` holds one action and the options request is a union listed by hand (`packages/contracts/src/staff.ts:154-157,173`); a step-up target id must be a lower-case uuid (`:147`), and a schema with a transform (`MediaId`, `packages/contracts/src/media.ts:20`) cannot be a params member. The only writers of `posts.state` set `deleted_by_author` (`apps/api/src/social/repo.ts:484,1093`); the author may delete a post in any other state (`:480-497`); the purge blanks every post and deletes every image row (`:1079-1121`; `apps/api/src/account/flows/deletion.ts:21-26`). The API updates only `body`, `state`, `deleted_at` and the four counters of `posts` (`repo.ts:469-562,1084-1102,1169-1172`). `lockLive` takes `FOR KEY SHARE` (`repo.ts:1160-1163`). `postAccess` (`apps/api/src/social/visibility.ts:18-23`) shows a post in any state but `visible` and `deleted_by_author` to its author, so a new state would fail open there; `visibleTo` (`repo.ts:318-321`) and `serve` (`apps/api/src/media/flows/serve.ts:31-35`) name only `withheld` and `removed` and fail closed; the export prints every post's body whatever its state (`repo.ts:976-990`, `apps/api/src/account/flows/export.ts:166-170`), and `readyImages` returns every ready image of the owner (`apps/api/src/media/repo.ts:131-138`). Images follow their post: visible ones are public for five minutes, withheld and removed ones go to their author only (`serve.ts:27-48`); views and the export carry every ready image (`media/repo.ts:114-138`). The console's policy allows images from its own origin only and its site proxies only `/api/staff` (`apps/admin/site-headers.mjs:9-10`; `infra/caddy/Caddyfile:82-99`); its source scans allow `href={` only in `src/nav.tsx` and no `src={` at all (`apps/admin/test/source.test.ts:65,73`); `ConsolePath` is pinned to three paths (`apps/admin/src/router.ts:7`). The staff route table pins the route list and its one path parameter, and refuses answer members named like `email`, `address`, `userId` or `accountId` (`apps/api/test/staff/route-table.test.ts:183,186-204,282`). Only the auth module holds addresses, the mailer and Turnstile (`apps/api/src/auth/index.ts:138-140,184`); its notices are best effort (`apps/api/src/auth/flows/notify.ts:4-11`); templates are a closed union of 25 (`apps/api/src/mail/mailer.ts:1-27`). `@korbat/rules` is a dependency of the API only (`apps/api/package.json:21`), and no source file imports it today. Profiles hold no image: `avatar_path` is only ever nulled (`repo.ts:1118`). drizzle-orm 0.45.2 runs every pending migration in one transaction (`node_modules/drizzle-orm/pg-core/dialect.js:60-71`): a value added with `ALTER TYPE ... ADD VALUE` to an enum created by an earlier, committed migration cannot be used before that transaction commits, while on a fresh install the type is created in the same transaction and the value is usable, so a lab run only on a fresh database would hide an upgrade failure.
- **One open case per target** (G3, PostgreSQL 18.6). A check-then-insert without a partial unique index made two open cases; with it the second insert waited and was refused (L6). `INSERT ... ON CONFLICT (target_type, target_id) WHERE closed_at IS NULL DO NOTHING` followed by an unlocked read let an R5 report attach to a case a moderator had just closed (L7); a migrator-owned `BEFORE INSERT` trigger on items that updates the open case and raises `serialization_failure` when it is closed made every such insert retry into a new case (L8, L10: 10,128 items, 34 retries, 0 failures). Decisions that answer through the sequence the moderator saw and refuse only when another decision landed: 18,900 items, 2,729 decisions, 0 violations of seven invariants (L11). Two notices naming the same two posts in opposite orders deadlocked; sorted by target they merged (L12). Without UPDATE on `cases`, `ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE` is refused for `korbat_api` even with no conflict; `DO NOTHING` works (L15).
- **The confirmed transaction on the API pool** (G2). A migrator-owned definer function in `public` reads `auth.users` and `auth.staff_keys` for `korbat_api` with 0001's grants unchanged, and the owner bypasses their RLS (3.1). `FOR SHARE` on the account's row, then on the key's row in a second statement, serialises a decision with a revocation or a take-down in either order; `FOR KEY SHARE` let a decision commit after its key was revoked; a single statement locking only the account let a revoked key through; key-first deadlocked with a revocation (3.2, S1 to S10). `korbat_api` may `set_config('lock_timeout', ..., true)`, which bounds every wait inside the definer guard and the chain's trigger (3.3). 3a's clock check works on the API role, and `RETURNING created_at` gives the exact stamp `audit-verify` compares (3.4).
- **Triggers, roles and statements** (G4, and the labs of review rounds 1 to 4, PostgreSQL 18.6). Deferred constraint triggers run at COMMIT after the audit insert while the head is held, add only ACCESS SHARE locks, and a caller can only make them earlier (`SET CONSTRAINTS ... IMMEDIATE`), never skip them (G4 5.3, 5.4); one can require that the transaction's last audit row names the event (5.5). `korbat_api` cannot disable a trigger, set `session_replication_role`, or lock a table it holds only INSERT and SELECT on (T15). A plain (not SECURITY DEFINER) trigger sees the role that ran the statement as `current_user`; `korbat_api`'s `SET ROLE`, `set_config('role', ...)` and `SET SESSION AUTHORIZATION` to the migrator are refused; and a plain trigger fired by a statement inside a migrator-owned SECURITY DEFINER function sees the migrator (labs of rounds 3 and 4). A logical restore into a fresh cluster restarts the transaction id counter while restored rows keep their stamps (measured: counter 773 after restoring stamps of 3761 and 3762), so a stored `xid8` is compared together with the transaction's start time (G4 6). An AFTER INSERT trigger on `decisions` sees none of its decision's actions, which are inserted after it (lab, round 4). Under READ COMMITTED each statement of a VOLATILE PL/pgSQL function takes a fresh snapshot, so a read in a statement of its own after a lock sees every row committed while the lock waited, while one statement whose subquery read a table before its row lock waited keeps the old snapshot (labs of rounds 2 to 4: `media_holds_apply`, `erase_case_evidence`, the restore of r4). Drizzle 0.45.2 nests transactions as savepoints that postgres 3.4.9 never releases (`node_modules/postgres/src/index.js:258,269,275-278`), so a row's `xmin` differs from `pg_current_xact_id()` after any nested block (G4 5.1).
- **Lock order** (G5, 60-second contention runs). A profile `FOR UPDATE` deadlocks with today's `deletePost` (post first, then the author's `post_count`) 32 to 38 times a minute; taking the author's row first removed every deletion cycle (V1fix, 4.2). Post-then-profile deadlocked 55 to 87 times a minute with likes and replies (V2, O2). Today's follow and unfollow already deadlock with each other with no moderation at all (B0). A transaction already holding a profile row upgrades without queueing behind a waiter (4.1). Column-level UPDATE grants keep `korbat_api` off a column while Drizzle's updates keep working (they name only the columns they set); inserts name every column, so INSERT stays table-level and a `BEFORE INSERT` trigger forces the guarded columns (P1 to P13). A definer bridge reading `auth.users` `FOR SHARE` decides "is this account staff" consistently against a concurrent promotion; `FOR KEY SHARE` does not (section 6).
- **Holds** (G6, lab E1 to E6). Every image file is deleted by a request file the API writes, which the worker obeys within about a second and cannot check (`apps/api/src/media/files.ts:180-183`; `apps/worker/src/loop.ts:68-83`); the reconcile pass sweeps any stored image older than an hour without a row (`apps/api/src/media/sweeper.ts:65-89`). So a hold must keep the `post_media` row: a column on the row was the only race-free form (a concurrent delete waits for the hold, re-reads and skips the row); a `BEFORE DELETE` trigger that returns NULL for a held row protects every present and future delete path, and must raise on a cascade (depth above 1), where returning NULL silently breaks foreign keys (E5d, E5b). A hold that comes after the author's deletion finds nothing, so holds belong in the intake transaction (E3b). A hold insert must lock the image rows first, in id order (lab, section 5, `MediaForCases`).
- **The freeze's keep trigger** (lab `korbat-scratch/research-3c/lab-gate-k`, PostgreSQL 18.6, four runs on 2026-10-03 under READ COMMITTED unless said; the machine was under load, so the times are upper bounds). A `BEFORE DELETE` row trigger on `post_media` that reads the freeze in a statement of its own sees a suspect item that committed while the delete waited for the intake's row locks: the ordered delete (`delete ... where id in (select id ... order by id for update)`) and a plain `delete ... where post_id = $1` both waited for the intake's `FOR KEY SHARE`, then deleted nothing and returned no id, for a post target and for an account target, whether the trigger read with `SELECT ... INTO` or with a plain assignment (T1 to T8, C1, C2). Without the intake's row locks the delete did not wait and won (T5), and an account item that committed with no lock while a purge of 20,000 rows ran kept only the 15,820 rows the purge reached after the commit (run 3, E); the intake's lock statement cost 77 ms and 287 kB of WAL at 5,000 rows and 102 ms and 1.1 MB at 20,000 (H). The same predicate as a filter of the deleting statement deleted the rows, since it runs on the statement's snapshot (T9; G6 E4 again). A predicate that found the post's author through the `posts` row did not refuse a cascade from a deleted post, because for the trigger's statement that row was already gone (T11); a core that reads no `posts` row, called with the image row's own `post_id` and `owner_id`, raised SQLSTATE 23001 at depth 2 for a cascade from a deleted post and from a deleted profile, under each kind of freeze (A1 to A6). An update guard refused moving an attached image, detaching it and attaching an upload to another account's post, and let an owner's own attach pass, so the owner of an attached row is its post's author (B1 to B4). Under REPEATABLE READ and SERIALIZABLE the trigger's read saw the transaction's old snapshot and the rows went; raising unless `transaction_isolation` is `read committed` kept them (run 4, I). As a SECURITY DEFINER function the trigger read the truth for a deleting role with no right on `cases` or `intake_items` (J). As three index-driven arms the predicate cost 6 buffer hits for a post nobody reported among 100,000 closed and 2,000 open cases (F). The purge of one owner took 0.5 to 0.7 s at 1,000 image rows, 2.3 to 3.6 s at 5,000 and 7 to 16 s at 20,000, kept or deleted alike (T13, D); an account's seal over image rows only took 0.3 s at 1,000, 1.5 s at 5,000 and 5.9 s at 20,000 (G).
- **Free text and digests** (G1). jsonb refuses the NUL character (U+0000) in a string and lone surrogates (L1 to L3); SQL, Node and WebCrypto compute the same salted digest (L9, N5); a CHECK can hold a stored text to its digest, and erasure then nulls text and salt (L10). Params of ids, enums, integers and hex digests survive the jsonb round trip with the same action hash (N3, N4).
- **Intake rules** (G9, lab T1 to T16). The CHECK constraints of section 6 accept every legitimate intake and refuse a CSAM notice carrying an account or a contact, an illegal-ground notice without explanation or bona fide statement, an old Transparency Database category and `OTHER_VIOLATION_TC` on an illegal ground; `korbat_api` cannot read a notifier contact and `korbat_auth` cannot read a notice (T13). Ordered by lane, the queue is served by one partial index without a sort (T15).
- **The law** (`law-3c.md`, re-read from the Publications Office on 2026-10-02). Art. 16 binds every host: a mechanism for anyone, electronic, "at least as easy" as the rules report (recital 50), facilitating the four elements of 16(2) with name and email asked but not required and not collected for child sexual abuse (EDPB Guidelines 3/2025 paras 29 to 31); a receipt and a decision "without undue delay" to whoever left contact details, the decision with redress and any automated means (16(4) to (6)); every notice processed (16(6)). Art. 17 binds: a statement for every restriction, "at the latest" when imposed, with the six points of 17(3). Art. 20 does not bind a micro platform (Art. 19(1)); korbat adopts its standards for the author's appeal and keeps for notifiers recital 58's human re-look at "no action" through re-examination (`law-3c.md` 5.1). Art. 23(2), suspending an abusive notifier's notices, does not bind and collides with 16(6). Art. 14(1) binds: the terms describe every moderation tool and step and the appeal's rules of procedure; Art. 14(4) asks for diligent, objective and proportionate enforcement.
